analysis.one_liner: Requires bank customers to opt in before overdraft fees can be charged, and bans misleading overdraft advertising.
analysis.headline: The bill received one subcommittee hearing but no markup and no vote, dying quietly when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required banks to get a customer's written consent before charging overdraft fees, and to warn the customer before completing a debit card or ATM transaction that would trigger a fee. It would have banned the practice of reordering transactions to manufacture overdraft fees, restricted ads that market overdrafts as short-term credit or call fee-laden accounts "free," and required ATMs to show the customer's real balance instead of a balance inflated by phantom overdraft credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking account customers who overdraw, especially low- and middle-income households living paycheck to paycheck. These are the people who get hit repeatedly by overdraft fees; the bill would have made the fees opt-in, made each fee visible before the transaction is completed, and stopped banks from rearranging the order of transactions to maximize the number of fees.

how_it_helps.text: No overdraft fee could be charged unless the customer first gave specific written consent to the fee program, with clear disclosure of the fee amount and when it applies [S3].

An ATM or debit card overdraft fee could only be charged if the customer had opted in and received a notice — with the fee amount — before irrevocably completing the transaction; if no notice was feasible, no fee could be charged [S3].

Depository institutions would be barred from a pattern or practice of delaying deposits or manipulating the order in which checks and debits post, when that manipulation produces overdrafts that trigger fees [S3].

Banks could not advertise an account as "free" if it carries overdraft fees, could not market overdrafts as a way to meet short-term credit needs or advance a customer's next paycheck, and could not claim all overdrafts will be covered while reserving discretion not to cover them [S3].
ATM balance inquiries would have to show the actual account balance only — not an inflated figure that includes overdraft credit the bank will charge for [S3].
The Federal Reserve would be authorized to restrict additional unfair or deceptive overdraft practices by regulation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit unions, and other depository institutions that rely on overdraft fees as a large and recurring source of revenue. Customers who want automatic overdraft coverage would have to affirmatively sign up for it.

drawbacks.text: Customers who do not opt in will still have transactions declined or returned unpaid, and the bill itself acknowledges returned-item fees still apply — the fee rules apply regardless of whether the fee equals what the bank charges for returning a check unpaid [S3]. Non-opt-in is not the same as free.

The bill does not abolish overdraft fees entirely: fees charged as an incidental accommodation (up to three per year), fees under an overdraft line of credit, and fees for transfers from the customer's own linked savings account are exempted from the definition [S3].

Banks argued overdraft fees pay for covering transactions when an account runs short, and that opt-in rules would push more transactions to be declined; some customers value automatic coverage and would now have to take a step to get it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary account holders clearly outweighs the cost. Overdraft programs were structured so that the bank's profit came from the customer's shortfall, often without the customer ever agreeing to the service, and the strongest honest objection — that some customers want automatic coverage — is answered by the bill itself, which lets those customers opt in. The main cost is to bank fee revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittee — one hearing was held, but no markup was ever scheduled and the bill never reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 12, 2009, by Rep. Carolyn Maloney with 16 Democratic cosponsors, and was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1].
One week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where a hearing was held; that was the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions kept collecting overdraft fee revenue with no new consent, disclosure, or transaction-ordering rules from Congress. Consumers got no relief from this bill; whatever curbs arrived later came from banking regulators acting on their own, not from legislation.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through referral to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee where a single hearing was held; no markup or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Banking industry groups
against.role: Commercial banks and credit union trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislative restrictions on overdraft fees, which were a major revenue source for depository institutions.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: Overdraft fees were a large, recurring revenue stream earned from customers' shortfalls; the bill would have made the fees opt-in, capped incidental fees at three per year, and banned the posting-order practices that multiply them. Banks' interest in keeping the fee stream ran directly against the account holders paying it.
They also collected overdraft fees and the bill applies to them, though smaller institutions argued they rely on the revenue more than big banks do. The rules apply regardless of size.
